outcome: The conjecture remains open. Every genuine numeric improvement to the known lower bound (0.01 -> (3-sqrt(5))/2 ~= 0.38197 -> ~0.38234 -> ~0.38271) was posted between November 2022 and June 2023, entirely before the 26 January 2024 freeze date. The only post-freeze events are a journal publication of already-known 2022 work, an arXiv metadata/write-up revision of an already-known 2022 bound, and a cluster of unverified 'full proof' preprints (2024 and 2026) that show no sign of expert acceptance and, in several cases, show clear hallmarks of low-quality or automated/crank submissions rather than mathematics.

disputes.summary: Multiple independent groups (Alweiss-Huang-Sellke, Chase-Lovett, Sawin, and separately Pebody) reached the (3-sqrt(5))/2 ~= 0.38197 bound within days of each other in November 2022, and Yu and Cambie independently reached ~0.3823 within weeks in December 2022. All of this predates the frozen revision and is background, not a post-window event, but it explains why the same numeric progress is attributed to different author sets across different secondary sources.

summary: The triage flagged three items, all of which turn out not to be genuine post-2024-01-26 progress on the conjecture itself once traced to primary sources. (1) The Alweiss-Huang-Sellke paper (arXiv:2211.11731, the source the triage's Feb-2025 EJC link actually corresponds to) proving the (3-sqrt(5))/2 ~= 0.38197 bound was submitted 21 November 2022 (v1-v3 all in Nov-Dec 2022); its only post-freeze event is formal journal publication in Electronic Journal of Combinatorics vol. 31(3) on 20 September 2024, which is a write-up/acceptance event for pre-existing 2022 mathematics, not a new result -- classified as open_stale territory for that specific bound, but since it was already public knowledge well before the freeze (and Wikipedia's Jan-2024 snapshot of this bullet doesn't cite a specific numeric constant to begin with), I record the problem's overall status as still open with no_change_found, folding this into background. (2) The 'improved bound' that the triage attributed to 'Cambie... Feb 2025' is arXiv:2212.12500, whose v1 was submitted 23 December 2022 and which reaches essentially the same ~0.3823 constant that Yu and Cambie both obtained in December 2022 (per Matthew Aldridge's timeline and cross-referenced against Liu's June 2023 paper, arXiv:2306.08824, which cites and improves on it to ~0.38271, itself also pre-freeze). The v2 revision dated 16 February 2025 is a metadata/text update to an already 2+-year-old preprint; I could not confirm it contains any bound beyond what existed in 2022, and no secondary source (survey, blog, or later citing paper) credits Cambie with a materially new numeric result after January 2024. (3) Two claimed full proofs were found: Roberto Demontis, 'The union-closed set conjecture is true' (arXiv:2405.03731, submitted 6 May 2024, single version, no retraction notice) and Jamolidin K. Abdurakhmanov, 'An Algorithmic Proof of Frankl's Union-Closed Sets Conjecture' (ResearchGate/HAL, dated 28 January 2026). Neither has any digestion, citation, or acceptance by an expert or venue that I could find (no Gil Kalai blog coverage, no Terence Tao mention, no MathOverflow discussion, no citing papers treating the conjecture as resolved) -- the conjecture continues to be described as open in every 2025-2026 secondary source I checked, including Gil Kalai's own 1 January 2026 'Combinatorics News' roundup, which discusses other combinatorics results but does not mention either claimed proof or treat the conjecture as settled. I also found a proliferation of Zenodo/ResearchGate/dev.to items around this problem ('The Reflection Restored -- A Machine-Certified Proof of Frankl's Conjecture via Collision-Restitution Invariants', an anonymous pseudonymous Zenodo upload tagged 'AI-augmented research'; 'A concavity obstruction and repaired support reductions in a Frankl entropy programme', an anonymous Zenodo record whose own description explicitly disclaims establishing any new bound, certificate, or peer review; and a GitHub repo 'frankl-conjecture-audit' cataloguing exactly this kind of claim) that read as automated or crank content rather than mathematics -- non-standard jargon ('collision-restitution invariants'), pseudonymous authorship, and self-disclaimed lack of any actual result. None of this constitutes a change to the problem under the scope rule of Section 3.1: an unverified, undigested preprint is not evidence the problem moved, and a self-disclaimed non-result certainly is not. No AI system was credited by any authors, in their own words, with producing mathematics that is part of a genuine, expert-accepted result on this problem -- the one AI-adjacent item found (the Zenodo 'AI-augmented research' tag) is on a paper that shows no sign of legitimacy and makes no first-person claim about what the AI produced, so ai_role is none rather than any of the AI-crediting codes.
competing_reading: One could argue the Alweiss-Huang-Sellke EJC journal publication (Sept 2024) or the Cambie arXiv v2 revision (Feb 2025) should be coded as 'progress' events with predates_frozen_revision noted, on the theory that a formal publication/revision date is itself a dateable event within the window even though the underlying mathematics is older. I chose not to do this because Section 6.3 instructs dating by the first public written argument, not the journal publication, specifically to avoid publication lag creating a false post-window event; treating a 2022 result's 2024/2025 formal write-up as 'progress' would overstate what happened since the freeze. If a future pass disagrees, the correct status would still be open_stale (not progress), since nothing about the bound changed.
what_would_settle_it: An expert digestion (a blog post by Kalai, Tao, or a subject specialist; a MathOverflow answer; or a citing paper treating the question as closed) of either the Demontis or Abdurakhmanov claimed proofs, in either direction -- confirming or refuting them -- would resolve whether this problem has moved past 'open'. Similarly, a citation trail showing Cambie's 2025 arXiv revision contains a numeric bound strictly better than Liu's 2023 ~0.38271 would establish genuine post-freeze quantitative progress, but I found no source making that claim.

I also could not fully verify whether Cambie's Feb 2025 arXiv v2 revision contains any numeric content beyond the ~0.3823 bound already known in December 2022, since I could not get clean text out of the PDF; my conclusion that it does not rests on the absence of any secondary source crediting Cambie with a newer, better constant.
